state.case_summary:
A 4-year-old African-American girl presented with a several-day history of cough, nasal congestion, intermittent fever, severe intermittent abdominal pain, and bloody stools. Her medical history included sickle cell disease, ulcerative colitis, and autoimmune hepatitis, treated with hydroxyurea, mesalamine, and azathioprine. On examination, she had clusters of 2–7 mm hemorrhagic vesicles on her palms, knees, and soles, and a tender, swollen right knee. Laboratory evaluation showed a C-reactive protein level of 31.1 mg/dL, leukocytosis (25.5 × 10^3 cells/µL), and anemia (hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL, hematocrit 18.7%). Bacterial and viral cultures of vesicle fluid were negative. Four months earlier, she had a similar episode attributed to a sickle cell crisis versus a flare of ulcerative colitis; biopsy at that time revealed a neutrophilic panniculitis. During the current admission, a repeat skin biopsy showed subcorneal and subepidermal edema and a dense acute neutrophilic infiltrate extending into adipose tissue and septa. Direct immunofluorescence of the lesion was negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Bowel-associated dermatosis-arthritis syndrome
B. Viral infections (eg, Coxsackie virus, varicella)
C. Sickle cell crisis versus ulcerative colitis flare
D. Bacterial infections (eg, subacute endocarditis, gonococcal sepsis)
E. Sweet syndrome
F. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis
G. Pyoderma gangrenosum
H. Rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis
